tool.name: DiversityIndices

summary.para: Neighborhood (focal) diversity of a categorical raster, where each cell holds a class value -- typically a species or a vegetation/community type. Over a moving neighborhood of any shape and size the tool measures how diverse the class values are and writes a continuous diversity raster. It offers the effective number of species (Hill numbers of order q -- the default and most defensible modern measure), Shannon's index, the Gini-Simpson index, and Simpson's concentration. It works on projected or geographic rasters and needs no Spatial Analyst. A modernized, generalized port of the Land Facet Corridor Designer's ArcMap Shannon's Index tool.

tool.usage:
What this tool does. For every cell it looks at the neighborhood around that cell, tallies how many cells belong to each class, turns those counts into proportions, and computes a diversity measure of the neighborhood. The result is a continuous raster: high values where many classes are present in balanced amounts, low values where one class dominates. The input must be categorical -- each distinct cell value is treated as its own class (a species, community, land-cover, or land-facet type). It is not meant for continuous rasters such as elevation; if the raster has thousands of unique values the tool assumes it is continuous and stops.
Classifying by an attribute field. A categorical raster often carries more than one classification in its attribute table: a Landfire EVT raster, or the tutorial's land cover raster with its 26 vegetation types and their 10 NLCD groups. The Classify by attribute field list offers Value (every distinct cell value is its own class, the original behavior) plus every text or integer column of the attribute table. Choose a column and every cell is relabeled by it before the neighborhood counting, so the diversity is measured over that column's classes -- 10 NLCD groups rather than 26 vegetation types. Cells sharing an entry become one class, a blank entry is its own class, and a cell value with no row in the table keeps a class of its own (the tool warns). A raster without an attribute table offers only Value. This is the same regrouping the Cross-Tab Statistics window offers for its raster variables. On a land facet raster keep Value: the facet is the cell value. Its attribute table also carries Category, which groups the facets by their first-pass class (four classes instead of eighteen), and Cluster, which is only the cluster number within each category and merges unrelated facets -- canyon-bottom cluster 1 with ridgetop cluster 1 -- into classes that mean nothing.
The effective number of species (the default). Shannon's and Simpson's indices are useful but they are not counts -- Shannon's index is an entropy and Simpson's is a probability, and neither is expressed in units you can intuitively compare. The effective number of species fixes this. It answers a single question: how many equally-common classes would give the same diversity as the actual, uneven neighborhood? A neighborhood of ten classes where one class holds 91 percent and the other nine hold 1 percent each has an effective number of only about 1.65 -- it behaves, diversity-wise, almost like a single-class neighborhood, because you almost always land in the dominant class. A neighborhood with ten equally-common classes has an effective number of exactly 10. The value is always between 1 (one class) and the class richness (all classes equally common), which is what makes it easy to interpret and to compare between places. These are the Hill numbers; Jost (2006) and Tuomisto (2010) call the result the "true diversity."
The order q. A single parameter, q, sets how much rare classes count toward the effective number: • q = 0 -- class richness: every class present counts fully, no matter how rare; the effective number equals the plain count of classes in the neighborhood. • q = 1 -- the exponential of Shannon's entropy: each class is weighted exactly in proportion to its abundance (the neutral, no-favorites choice). This is the default, and the value most often meant by "the effective number of species." • q = 2 -- the inverse Simpson index: common classes dominate and rare ones barely register.
Any non-negative q is allowed, not just 0, 1, and 2. As q increases the effective number can only stay the same or fall, because rare classes are progressively discounted. Running the tool at q = 0, 1, and 2 and comparing gives a "diversity profile": a steep drop from q = 0 to q = 2 is the fingerprint of dominance (a few classes run the show), while a flat profile means the classes are evenly mixed. Because the inverse Simpson index is exactly the effective number at q = 2, it is offered here rather than duplicated as a separate Simpson option.
The other measures. Shannon's Index (H) is the classic diversity entropy, computed with the natural logarithm; higher means more diverse. Its exponential is the effective number at q = 1. Gini-Simpson (1 - sum of squared proportions) is the probability that two cells drawn at random from the neighborhood belong to different classes; it runs from 0 (one class) toward 1 (many even classes) and is the measure most people mean by "Simpson's diversity index." Simpson's Concentration (the sum of squared proportions) is Simpson's original 1949 definition -- the probability that two random cells are the same class -- so it is a dominance measure in which higher means less diverse; its symbology ramp is reversed so that greener still reads as more diverse.
Neighborhoods and units. All Focal-Statistics neighborhood shapes are available: Rectangle (width x height), Circle (radius), Annulus (inner and outer radius), Wedge (radius plus start and end angles, counter-clockwise from east), and Irregular / Weight from an ASCII kernel file (first line "ncols nrows", then the matrix; Irregular = 0/1, Weight = weights). Sizes are given in Cells or in a ground unit (Meters, Kilometers, Feet, Miles). On a projected raster the neighborhood is a fixed number of cells; on a geographic (latitude/longitude) raster, where cell size on the ground changes with latitude, a ground-unit neighborhood is sized geodesically per row -- the same treatment the other neighborhood tools in this toolbox use. Kernel-file neighborhoods are defined in cells. A weighted (Weight) kernel produces weighted proportions, which all four measures accept.
NoData. NoData cells are ignored within each neighborhood by default, so a neighborhood is summarized from whatever valid cells it contains. Turn on "Return NoData if the neighborhood includes any NoData cell" to instead write NoData wherever any NoData cell falls inside the neighborhood (edges that simply run off the raster do not count as NoData). A cell with no valid neighbor at all is always NoData.
Performance. The tool makes one neighborhood pass per class, so run time grows with the number of classes; a handful to a few dozen classes (typical for species or community rasters) is fast, hundreds is slower, and the tool warns past 500 classes and stops past 5000. This tool honors no geoprocessing environments.
References. Diversity measures: Shannon, C.E. 1948, "A mathematical theory of communication," Bell System Technical Journal 27:379-423 (https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x); Simpson, E.H. 1949, "Measurement of diversity," Nature 163:688 (https://doi.org/10.1038/163688a0); Hill, M.O. 1973, "Diversity and evenness: a unifying notation and its consequences," Ecology 54:427-432 (https://doi.org/10.2307/1934352); Jost, L. 2006, "Entropy and diversity," Oikos 113:363-375 (https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2006.0030-1299.14714.x); Tuomisto, H. 2010, "A consistent terminology for quantifying species diversity? Yes, it does exist," Oecologia 164:853-860 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00442-010-1812-0). Corridor Designer tools: Majka, D., J. Jenness, and P. Beier. 2007, "CorridorDesigner: ArcGIS tools for designing and evaluating corridors" (http://corridordesign.org). Land Facet Corridor Designer: Beier, P., and B. Brost. 2010, "Use of land facets to plan for climate change: conserving the arenas, not the actors," Conservation Biology 24:701-710 (https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1523-1739.2010.01422.x); Jenness, J., B. Brost, and P. Beier. 2013, "Land Facet Corridor Designer: Extension for ArcGIS," Jenness Enterprises (http://www.jennessent.com/arcgis/land_facets.htm).

dialogReference.para: A single-band categorical raster: each cell holds a class value, typically a species or vegetation/community code. Every distinct value is treated as its own class. Integer rasters are expected; a floating-point raster with non-integer values still works but each unique value becomes a class, and a raster with thousands of unique values is assumed to be continuous and rejected.

param.name: class_field
param.displayname: Classify by attribute field (Value = each cell value is its own class)

dialogReference.para: Which column of the raster's attribute table defines the classes. Value (the default) treats every distinct cell value as its own class. Any text or integer column of the attribute table can be chosen instead: every cell is then relabeled by that column before the diversity is measured, so a vegetation raster of 26 types with an NLCD column is measured as its 10 NLCD groups. Cells sharing an entry become one class; a blank entry is its own class; a cell value with no row in the table keeps a class of its own (with a warning). The list is filled from the raster you choose and is disabled, holding only Value, when the raster has no attribute table. The same regrouping the Cross-Tab Statistics window offers. On a land facet raster keep Value: the facet is the cell value; Category groups the facets by their first-pass class, and Cluster is only the cluster number within each category, which merges unrelated facets.
The output continuous diversity raster. A name is suggested from the input and the chosen measure. A folder path typed without an extension is written as a GeoTIFF.
Which diversity measure to compute (one per run):

bulletList.bullet_item: Effective Number of Species (Hill numbers -- the default; see the Order (q) parameter) reports the number of equally-common classes that would give the same diversity.
Shannon's Index (H) is the classic entropy (natural log).
Gini-Simpson (1 - D) is the probability that two random cells differ in class.
Simpson's Concentration (D) is Simpson's original dominance measure, where higher means less diverse. The inverse Simpson index is the effective number at q = 2.

dialogReference.para: The order q, used only for the Effective Number of Species. It controls how much rare classes count:

bulletList.bullet_item: q = 0 is class richness (all classes count fully).
q = 1 (the default) is the exponential of Shannon's entropy, weighting each class by its abundance.
q = 2 is the inverse Simpson index, dominated by the common classes.

dialogReference.para: Any non-negative value is allowed. Higher q gives less weight to rare classes, so the effective number stays the same or decreases as q rises.
The neighborhood shape: Rectangle, Circle, Annulus, Wedge, or Irregular / Weight (from a kernel file). The relevant size parameters below become active for the chosen shape.

The units for the neighborhood size: Cells, or a ground unit (Meters, Kilometers, Feet, Miles). On a geographic raster a ground unit is sized geodesically per row. Not used for kernel-file neighborhoods, which are defined in cells.
The neighborhood radius (Circle and Wedge), in the chosen units.
The rectangle width, in the chosen units (Rectangle neighborhood).
The rectangle height, in the chosen units (Rectangle neighborhood).
The inner radius of the ring (Annulus neighborhood), in the chosen units. Cells inside this radius are excluded.
The outer radius of the ring (Annulus neighborhood), in the chosen units. Must be greater than the Inner radius.
The wedge's starting angle in degrees, measured counter-clockwise from east (Wedge neighborhood). The wedge spans counter-clockwise from the start angle to the end angle.
The wedge's ending angle in degrees, measured counter-clockwise from east (Wedge neighborhood).

An ASCII kernel file for the Irregular or Weight neighborhood: the first line is "ncols nrows", followed by the matrix. Irregular files use 0 (excluded) and 1 (included); Weight files hold weights (0 = excluded), which produce weighted class proportions. The kernel is centered on each cell and defined in cells.

param.name: exclude_null
param.displayname: Return NoData if the neighborhood includes any NoData cell

dialogReference.para: If checked, any neighborhood that contains a NoData cell is written as NoData. If unchecked (the default), NoData cells are simply ignored and the neighborhood is summarized from its valid cells. Edges that run off the raster are not treated as NoData.

scriptExample.title: Diversity Indices example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: The effective number of species (q = 1) over a 3-cell circle, then class richness (effective number, q = 0), then the Gini-Simpson index over a 1000 m circle on a geographic raster. Valid index values are exactly: "Effective Number of Species", "Shannon's Index (H)", "Gini-Simpson Index (1 - D)", "Simpson's Concentration (D)". neighborhood: "Rectangle", "Circle", "Annulus", "Wedge", "Irregular", "Weight". nbr_units: "Cells", "Meters", "Kilometers", "Feet", "Miles". The q argument is used only for the effective number. Unused neighborhood arguments may be left as-is; only the ones for the chosen shape are read.
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
# Effective number of species (Hill q=1) over a 3-cell-radius circle arcpy.jenness.DiversityIndices( "species.tif", "species_EffNum_q1.tif", "Effective Number of Species", 1, "Circle", "Cells", 3)
# Class richness (effective number at q=0) arcpy.jenness.DiversityIndices( "species.tif", "species_Richness.tif", "Effective Number of Species", 0, "Circle", "Cells", 3)
# Gini-Simpson index over a 1000 m circle (geographic raster: sized per row) arcpy.jenness.DiversityIndices( "communities.tif", "communities_GiniSimpson.tif", "Gini-Simpson Index (1 - D)", 1, "Circle", "Meters", 1000)
